nodes.label: Power Sharing
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Distribution of power among different organs, levels, and social groups of government. Two justifications: prudential (reduces conflict, ensures stability) and moral (the very spirit of democracy). Citizens acquire a stake in the system through participation.

nodes.label: Prudential Reasons for Power Sharing
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Practical reasons: reduces possibility of social conflict, ensures political stability, prevents tyranny of majority. Imposing majority will may bring short-term gains but undermines national unity in long run. Sri Lanka's civil war illustrates the danger of not sharing power.

nodes.label: Moral Reasons for Power Sharing
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Power sharing is the very spirit of democracy. Democratic rule involves sharing power with those affected by it. People have right to be consulted on governance. A legitimate government is one where citizens acquire a stake through participation.

nodes.label: Majoritarianism
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Belief that the majority community should rule in whichever way it wants, disregarding wishes and needs of minorities. Sri Lanka's Sinhala-dominated policies are the classic example. Contrasted with power sharing which accommodates diversity.

nodes.label: Forms of Power Sharing
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Four forms: (1) horizontal - among legislature, executive, judiciary (separation of powers); (2) vertical - among central, state, local governments (federalism); (3) among social groups - reserved constituencies, community governments; (4) among political parties, pressure groups, movements.

nodes.label: Horizontal Power Sharing
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Distribution of power among different organs of government at the same level - legislature, executive, and judiciary. Each organ checks the others (checks and balances). Ensures no single organ can exercise unlimited power.

nodes.label: Vertical Power Sharing (Federalism)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Distribution of power among different levels of government - central, state/provincial, and local. Higher and lower levels have their own jurisdictions. Constitution guarantees existence and authority of each level. India follows this model.

nodes.label: Checks and Balances
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: System where each organ of government can check the others and maintain balance of power. Legislature controls executive through no-confidence motions. Judiciary can strike down laws (judicial review). Executive implements but cannot make laws unilaterally.

nodes.label: Ethnic Composition and Conflict
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Social division based on shared culture and common descent. Both Belgium and Sri Lanka have complex ethnic compositions. How a country handles ethnic diversity - through accommodation or domination - determines social peace or conflict.

nodes.label: Power Sharing Among Social Groups
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Mechanisms to give representation to disadvantaged social groups: reserved constituencies for SC/ST, community governments for linguistic groups (Belgium), consociational arrangements. Prevents domination by any single social group.

nodes.label: Power Sharing Among Parties and Groups
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Democracy allows multiple political parties, pressure groups, and movements to compete and share power. Coalitions, opposition parties, and interest groups ensure that power does not concentrate in one political formation.

nodes.label: Federalism
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: System of government where power is divided between a central authority and constituent units. Dual objectives: safeguard and promote unity while accommodating regional diversity. Requires mutual trust and agreement to live together. India is a federation though Constitution uses 'Union of States'.

nodes.label: Key Features of Federalism
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Seven features: (1) two or more tiers of government, (2) each tier has own jurisdiction, (3) constitutionally guaranteed, (4) fundamental provisions cannot be unilaterally changed, (5) courts interpret constitution and resolve disputes, (6) revenue sources specified for each level, (7) dual objectives of unity and diversity.

nodes.label: Unitary System
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: System where either there is only one level of government or sub-units are subordinate to the central government. Central government can pass orders to provincial/local governments. Sri Lanka is an example. Contrasted with federal system.

nodes.label: Coming Together Federation
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Independent states voluntarily come together to form a larger unit, pooling sovereignty while retaining identity for security. USA, Switzerland, Australia are examples. Constituent states usually have equal power and are strong vis-a-vis federal government.

nodes.label: Holding Together Federation
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A large country decides to divide power between constituent states and national government. India, Spain, Belgium are examples. Central government tends to be more powerful. Different units may have unequal powers. Some units granted special status.

nodes.label: Union List
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Subjects of national importance on which only the Union Government can legislate. Includes defence, foreign affairs, banking, communications, currency. Ensures uniform policy on matters requiring national coordination.

nodes.label: State List
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Subjects of state and local importance on which only State Governments can legislate. Includes police, trade, commerce, agriculture, irrigation. Ensures states have autonomy in local governance matters.

nodes.label: Concurrent List
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Subjects of common interest on which both Union and State Governments can legislate. Includes education, forest, trade unions, marriage, adoption, succession. In case of conflict, Union law prevails.

nodes.label: Residuary Powers
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Power to legislate on subjects not in any of the three lists. In India, Union Government has residuary powers. Covers new subjects like computer software that emerged after the Constitution was made.

nodes.label: Centre-State Relations
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Constitution distributes powers between centre and states through three lists. Amendment requires two-thirds majority plus ratification by half the states. Judiciary arbitrates disputes. Financial autonomy through specified revenue sources. Restructuring strengthened federalism.

nodes.label: Special Status States
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Some states enjoy special provisions under the Constitution. Jammu and Kashmir had its own Constitution and many Indian laws did not apply without state assembly approval. Similar provisions exist for northeastern states. Reflects 'holding together' nature of Indian federalism.

nodes.label: Social Differences
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Differences among people based on accident of birth (caste, race, gender) or choice (religion, occupation, political views). Not every social difference leads to division. People have multiple overlapping identities that can unite or divide.

nodes.label: Overlapping Social Differences
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: When one social difference is reinforced by another (e.g., in Northern Ireland, class and religion overlap - Catholics are poor, Protestants are rich). Creates deep social divisions that are harder to accommodate. More likely to produce social conflict.

nodes.label: Cross-Cutting Social Differences
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: When social differences cross-cut one another (e.g., in Netherlands, Catholics and Protestants are both rich and poor). Members of one group are also members of other groups. Easier to accommodate. Less likely to cause deep conflict.

nodes.label: Social Divisions and Politics
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Three outcomes when social divisions enter politics: (1) democracy strengthened when disadvantaged groups express grievances, (2) social divisions can be accommodated if parties don't make exclusive demands, (3) social divisions can threaten national unity if demands are non-negotiable.

nodes.label: Multiple Identities
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Every individual has more than one identity (gender, religion, region, language, caste, class). These identities can align or cross-cut. A person can feel strong affinity with someone of different nationality but similar interests, while feeling distant from someone of same nationality.

nodes.label: Politics as Vehicle for Social Change
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Political expression of social divisions helps disadvantaged groups express grievances. Brings issues to the political agenda. Leads to social change through legislation and policy. Without political expression, injustices remain unaddressed.

nodes.label: Accommodation vs Domination
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Two ways of responding to social diversity: accommodation (Belgium model - sharing power, respecting diversity) or domination (Sri Lanka model - majority imposing its will). Accommodation strengthens democracy; domination leads to conflict.

nodes.label: Homogeneous vs Heterogeneous Society
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Homogeneous societies have little social diversity (e.g., Japan). Heterogeneous societies have diverse populations along multiple lines. Most countries are heterogeneous. Migrant societies (USA, Australia) became diverse through immigration. All societies face some social divisions.

nodes.label: Gender Division in Politics
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Hierarchical social division based on social expectations, not biology. Sexual division of labour assigns domestic work to women. Women constitute half of humanity but role in politics minimal. Feminist movements fought for equal political, legal, and social rights.

nodes.label: Sexual Division of Labour
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: System where household work is done by women while men work outside. Women's work remains unpaid and invisible. Indian women work one hour more daily than men on average but earn less. Equal Wages Act exists but is poorly implemented.

nodes.label: Feminist Movement
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Movements by women and men who believe in equal rights and opportunities for women. Demanded extension of voting rights, political and legal equality, and equal status in personal and family life. Led to women's participation in public life, professions, and politics.

nodes.label: Women's Political Representation
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: India's record: Women's Reservation Bill for 33% seats in Parliament/state legislatures pending for years. One-third seats reserved in local bodies (panchayats/municipalities) has been successful. Scandinavian countries lead in women's public participation.

nodes.label: Communalism
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Belief that religion is the principal basis of social community. Communal politics involves demands of one religious group at the expense of another. Can range from religious prejudice to use of religion in politics to communal violence. Constitution provides secular framework to counter it.

nodes.label: Secularism in India
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Indian secularism means: no official religion, freedom to profess any religion, no discrimination based on religion, state can intervene in religious matters for social reform (like banning untouchability or allowing temple entry). Different from Western separation of church and state.

nodes.label: Caste and Politics
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Caste groups try to grow larger by forming caste coalitions. Political parties choose candidates from different castes to win. No party wins votes of all caste members, and no caste votes as a block. Caste politics can bring disadvantaged groups to power but also distracts from real issues.

nodes.label: Caste Inequality in India
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Despite constitutional prohibition, caste discrimination persists. Upper castes dominate high-income positions. SC/ST and OBC lag in education and employment. Untouchability practices continue in some areas. Reservations attempt to address this but debate continues.

nodes.label: Religion and Politics
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Not all expression of religion in politics is communalism. People's political preferences are influenced by religious beliefs. Positive when religion promotes ethical politics. Communal when religion is used to mobilise against another community. Constitution separates religion from state power.

nodes.label: OBC Reservation
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Other Backward Classes (OBC) identified by Mandal Commission. 27% reservation in central government jobs and educational institutions. Creamy layer (well-off among OBCs) excluded from benefits. Extended to local body elections in many states.

nodes.label: Caste Does Not Determine Election Results
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Evidence shows: no party wins votes of all voters from one caste; no caste/community is large enough to win on its own; ruling party routinely loses despite caste arithmetic. Multiple factors including performance, alliances, and economic issues determine election outcomes.

nodes.label: Women's Reservation in Local Bodies
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: One-third of seats in panchayats and municipalities reserved for women under 73rd and 74th Amendments. Has led to over 10 lakh elected women representatives. One of the most successful affirmative action measures in the world.

nodes.label: State/Regional Parties
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Parties with influence mainly in one state or region. Over 750 registered parties in India. Examples: BJD (Odisha), TDP (Andhra), DMK/AIADMK (Tamil Nadu). Have risen in importance since 1990s with coalition era. Together serve as effective opposition.

nodes.label: Reforms in Political Parties
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Constitutional and legal reforms: anti-defection law, mandatory organisational elections, financial disclosure, candidate affidavit system. People's initiatives: pressure groups monitoring parties, voter awareness campaigns, right to reject (NOTA). Reform is gradual and ongoing.

nodes.label: Alliances and Fronts
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Several parties join hands for contesting elections and winning power. In India: NDA (BJP-led), UPA (Congress-led), Left Front (CPI-M led). Alliance politics became central since 1990s as no single party consistently wins majority.

nodes.label: Dignity of the Individual
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Democracy best suited to promote dignity and freedom of citizens. Long struggles for women's dignity and against caste discrimination show that once principle is recognised, legal/constitutional changes follow. Democracies have this moral advantage.

nodes.label: Challenge of Deepening
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Strengthening democratic institutions and practices so people can realise their expectations. Means strengthening institutions for people's participation and control. Requires reducing control of rich and powerful over governmental decisions. Every democracy faces this.

nodes.label: Legal-Constitutional Reforms
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Changes in law to overcome challenges: anti-defection law, mandatory disclosure by candidates, gender quotas, state funding of elections, regulation of party organisation. Legal changes alone are insufficient; democratic practice must also change.

nodes.label: Challenge of Inclusion
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Ensuring that all social groups - women, minorities, indigenous peoples, marginalised communities - have equal voice in democracy. Extension of federal principle, decentralisation, and affirmative action are tools for inclusion.

nodes.label: Challenge of People's Participation
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Formal democracy requires active citizen participation beyond voting. Includes joining parties, forming associations, engaging in public debate, filing RTI, PIL. Apathy and disengagement weaken democracy. Education and awareness promote participation.

nodes.label: Constitution
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A body of fundamental principles according to which a state is governed. Serves five functions: coordination, power allocation, limitation of government, enabling aspirations, and establishing fundamental identity. India's is one of the longest written constitutions in the world.

nodes.label: Preamble
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Opening statement of the Constitution declaring India a Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic. Contains key values: justice, liberty, equality, fraternity. 'Socialist' and 'Secular' added by 42nd Amendment (1976). Based on the Objective Resolution.

nodes.label: Borrowed Features
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Indian Constitution draws from multiple sources: British (parliamentary system, rule of law), US (fundamental rights, judicial review, federal structure), Irish (DPSP), Canadian (federation with strong centre), Australian (concurrent list), Weimar (emergency provisions), South African (amendment procedure).

nodes.label: Fundamental Rights
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Part III of Constitution (Articles 12-35). Justiciable rights that limit government power. Six categories: equality, freedom, against exploitation, religion, cultural/educational, constitutional remedies. Can be suspended during Emergency except Articles 20-21.

nodes.label: Directive Principles of State Policy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Part IV of Constitution (Articles 36-51). Non-justiciable guidelines for governance. Direct the state to promote welfare, reduce inequality, ensure adequate livelihood. Inspired by Irish Constitution. Complement fundamental rights.

nodes.label: Federal Structure
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Constitution establishes a federal system with division of powers between Centre and States. Three lists: Union, State, Concurrent. Strong centre with unitary features in emergencies. Borrowed from Canadian model (federation with strong centre).

nodes.label: Secularism in Constitution
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: No state religion. State treats all religions equally. Freedom of religion guaranteed under Articles 25-28. 'Secular' explicitly added to Preamble by 42nd Amendment 1976, but secular character was implicit from the beginning.

nodes.label: Universal Adult Franchise
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Every citizen above 18 years has right to vote regardless of caste, religion, gender, education, or property. Bold decision for newly independent India with mass illiteracy. Originally 21 years, reduced to 18 by 61st Amendment 1988.

nodes.label: Single Citizenship
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Unlike US federal model, India has single citizenship. Every Indian is a citizen of India, not of any particular state. Promotes national unity and integration.

nodes.label: Rule of Law
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Principle that law governs the nation, not arbitrary decisions. No person above the law. Government authority exercised only in accordance with law. Borrowed from British constitutional tradition (Dicey).

nodes.label: Separation of Powers
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Legislature makes laws, Executive implements, Judiciary interprets. India follows a modified separation — not as strict as US model. Parliamentary system inherently fuses legislature and executive. Checks and balances ensure no organ becomes supreme.

nodes.label: Right to Equality
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Equality before law (Art 14), prohibition of discrimination (Art 15), equal opportunity in public employment (Art 16), abolition of untouchability (Art 17), abolition of titles (Art 18).

nodes.label: Article 14 - Equality Before Law
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Equality before law (British concept) and equal protection of laws (American 14th Amendment concept). Permits reasonable classification but not class legislation. State can treat unequals unequally.

nodes.label: Right to Freedom
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Six freedoms under Art 19 (speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession). Art 20: protection against conviction. Art 21: right to life and personal liberty. Art 22: protection against arbitrary arrest.

nodes.label: Right to Constitutional Remedies
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Article 32: Right to move Supreme Court for enforcement of fundamental rights. Ambedkar called it 'the heart and soul of the Constitution'. SC can issue writs: habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo warranto.

nodes.label: Constitutional Writs
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Five writs: Habeas Corpus (produce the body), Mandamus (command to perform duty), Prohibition (prohibit lower court), Certiorari (quash lower court order), Quo Warranto (by what authority). SC under Art 32, HC under Art 226.

nodes.label: Directive Principles of State Policy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Non-justiciable guidelines for state. Three categories: socialistic (Art 38-39, 41-43), Gandhian (Art 40, 43, 46-48), liberal-intellectual (Art 44-45, 48A, 49-51). Not enforceable in court but fundamental in governance.

nodes.label: Uniform Civil Code
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Article 44 directs state to secure a uniform civil code for all citizens throughout India. One of the most debated DPSPs. Tension between religious freedom and national uniformity. Not yet implemented.

nodes.label: Fundamental Duties
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Article 51A — added by 42nd Amendment 1976 on Swaran Singh Committee recommendation. Originally 10 duties, 11th added by 86th Amendment 2002. Non-justiciable. Include respecting Constitution, national flag, defending country, promoting harmony.

nodes.label: FR-DPSP Tension
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Ongoing debate whether FRs or DPSPs should prevail when they conflict. Golaknath case (1967): FRs cannot be amended. Kesavananda Bharati (1973): FRs can be amended but basic structure cannot. Minerva Mills (1980): Harmony between FR and DPSP is basic structure.

nodes.label: Right to Property (Removed)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Originally a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31. Removed from Part III by 44th Amendment 1978. Now only a legal right under Article 300A. Removed to enable land reform and redistribution.

nodes.label: Reasonable Restrictions
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Article 19(2)-(6) allow state to impose reasonable restrictions on freedoms. Grounds include: sovereignty, security, public order, decency, morality, contempt of court, defamation, incitement to offence. Restrictions must be reasonable, not arbitrary.

nodes.label: Elections in India
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Democratic elections based on universal adult franchise. Regular elections held every 5 years for Lok Sabha and State Assemblies. Elections are the mechanism through which people choose representatives and hold them accountable.

nodes.label: First Past the Post (FPTP)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Electoral system used for Lok Sabha and State Assembly elections. Country divided into constituencies, candidate with most votes wins. Simple, clear winner, but may not reflect overall vote share proportionally. Favours major parties.

nodes.label: Proportional Representation
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: System where seats are allocated proportional to vote share. Used for Rajya Sabha and Presidential elections in India (single transferable vote variant). Ensures minority representation but complex and no direct constituency link.

nodes.label: Universal Adult Franchise
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Article 326: Every citizen 18+ has right to vote (reduced from 21 by 61st Amendment 1988). No discrimination on basis of religion, race, caste, sex, or literacy. One person one vote principle. Foundation of Indian democracy.

nodes.label: Reserved Constituencies
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Constituencies reserved for SC and ST candidates to ensure their representation. Articles 330/332. Only candidates from SC/ST can contest from reserved seats but all voters vote. Extended periodically — currently till 2030.

nodes.label: Model Code of Conduct
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Rules governing parties and candidates during elections. Not statutory but enforced by EC. Prohibits use of government resources for campaigning, bans appeals to religion/caste, restricts government announcements. Comes into effect from date of announcement.

nodes.label: Rajya Sabha Elections
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Members elected by elected members of State Legislative Assemblies using single transferable vote (proportional representation). 1/3 members retire every 2 years. 12 members nominated by President. Not subject to dissolution.

nodes.label: Constituency System
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: India divided into 543 Lok Sabha constituencies and varying state assembly constituencies. Each constituency elects one representative. Territorial constituencies ensure geographic representation.

nodes.label: Election Petition
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Challenge to election results filed in High Court. Grounds include corrupt practices, non-compliance with election law, improper acceptance/rejection of nomination. HC decision appealable to SC.

nodes.label: Nomination and Candidature
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Candidates must file nomination papers with returning officer. Security deposit required (Rs 25,000 for general, Rs 12,500 for SC/ST). Minimum age: 25 for Lok Sabha/Assembly, 30 for Rajya Sabha. Must be registered voter.

nodes.label: Collective Responsibility
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Council of Ministers collectively responsible to Lok Sabha (Art 75(3)). If Lok Sabha passes no-confidence motion, entire council resigns. Ministers must support cabinet decisions publicly even if they disagreed privately.

nodes.label: Presidential Veto
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: President can withhold assent (absolute veto), return bill for reconsideration (suspensive veto — overridden if passed again), or keep bill pending indefinitely (pocket veto). Cannot return money bills. Constitutional amendment bills must be assented.

nodes.label: No-Confidence Motion
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Motion in Lok Sabha to remove Council of Ministers. Needs support of minimum 50 members to be admitted. If passed by simple majority, PM and entire council must resign. Only in Lok Sabha, not Rajya Sabha.

nodes.label: Independence of the Judiciary
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The judiciary must function free from interference by the executive and legislature. Ensured through security of tenure, fixed service conditions, salaries charged on Consolidated Fund, and a difficult removal procedure. Independence does not mean absence of accountability -- judiciary remains accountable to the Constitution.

nodes.label: Single Integrated Judicial System
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Unlike some federal countries, India does not have separate state courts. The judiciary is a single integrated system with Supreme Court at the apex, High Courts below, and district/subordinate courts at the base. Lower courts function under superintendence of higher courts.

nodes.label: Original Jurisdiction of Supreme Court
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Cases directly heard by the Supreme Court without prior hearing by lower courts. Covers disputes between Union and States, and among States themselves (federal disputes). SC acts as umpire in federal matters. Neither High Courts nor lower courts can deal with such cases.

nodes.label: Writ Jurisdiction
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Supreme Court under Article 32 and High Courts under Article 226 can issue writs for enforcement of fundamental rights. Five types of writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo Warranto. Article 32 is itself a fundamental right (right to constitutional remedies). Article 226 has wider scope.

nodes.label: Appellate Jurisdiction of Supreme Court
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: SC is the highest court of appeal in civil, criminal, and constitutional cases. Appeals from High Courts require certification that the case involves substantial question of law. In criminal cases involving death sentence, appeal can be made directly. SC can also grant Special Leave to Appeal (Article 136) from any court or tribunal.

nodes.label: Advisory Jurisdiction of Supreme Court
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Under Article 143, the President can refer questions of law or fact of public importance to the Supreme Court for its opinion. However, the SC is not bound to give advice, and the President is not bound to accept such advice. Helps government seek legal opinion before action and prevents unnecessary litigation.

nodes.label: Habeas Corpus
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Literally means to have the body. Issued to produce a person detained unlawfully before the court. Protects personal liberty against arbitrary detention. Can be issued by both Supreme Court and High Courts. Most powerful safeguard of individual liberty.

nodes.label: Mandamus
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Literally means we command. Issued to direct a public official or government body to perform a duty they have failed to perform. Cannot be issued against a private individual or the President/Governors for their discretionary functions.

nodes.label: Quo Warranto
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Literally means by what authority. Issued to inquire into the legality of a persons claim to a public office. Prevents illegal usurpation of public office. Can only be issued against substantive public offices of a permanent character created by statute or Constitution.

nodes.label: Judicial Review
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Power of the Supreme Court and High Courts to examine the constitutionality of legislative enactments and executive orders. If found inconsistent with the Constitution, the law is declared unconstitutional and void (Article 13). Term judicial review is not mentioned in Constitution but is implicit. Extends to both fundamental rights violations and federal distribution of powers.

nodes.label: Judicial Activism
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The proactive role of the judiciary in protecting rights and ensuring government accountability, going beyond the traditional role of merely adjudicating disputes. Flourished in India through PIL since late 1970s. Has expanded scope of rights, forced executive accountability, but also raised concerns about blurring separation of powers.

nodes.label: Public Interest Litigation (PIL)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Also called Social Action Litigation (SAL). Allows any public-spirited citizen to file a case on behalf of those who cannot approach courts themselves. Emerged around 1979. Court began accepting cases based on newspaper reports and postal complaints. Expanded the idea of rights to include clean air, unpolluted water, decent living. Chief instrument of judicial activism in India.

nodes.label: Appointment of Judges
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: SC and HC judges are appointed by the President. For CJI, convention of appointing seniormost judge was followed (broken in 1973 for A.N. Ray and 1975 for M.H. Beg superseding Justice Khanna). Other SC judges appointed after consulting CJI. Through three Judges Cases (1982, 1993, 1998), the collegium system evolved where CJI and 4 senior judges recommend appointments.

nodes.label: Removal of Judges (Impeachment)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: SC and HC judges can be removed only on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity. Requires special majority in both Houses of Parliament (majority of total membership AND two-thirds of members present and voting). Only one case came up -- Justice Ramaswamy (1993) -- motion got two-thirds of those present but not majority of total strength due to Congress abstention.

nodes.label: Contempt of Court
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Supreme Court and High Courts have power to punish for contempt of themselves. Two types: civil contempt (disobedience of court orders) and criminal contempt (scandalizing the court). Acts as protection for judges from unfair criticism. Parliament cannot discuss conduct of judges except during removal proceedings.

nodes.label: Basic Structure Doctrine
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Judicial innovation from Kesavananda Bharati case (1973). Constitution basic features cannot be amended even by Parliament. Not mentioned anywhere in the Constitution -- emerged from judicial interpretation. Includes supremacy of Constitution, republican and democratic form of government, secular character, separation of powers, federal character, unity and sovereignty of India, judicial review, and fundamental rights.

nodes.label: Right to Property -- Parliament vs Judiciary
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Central issue in Parliament-Judiciary conflict. Parliament wanted to restrict property rights for land reforms. Court held Parliament cannot abridge fundamental rights. Kesavananda case (1973) held property right not part of basic structure. 44th Amendment (1978) removed right to property from fundamental rights, making it only a legal right under Article 300A.

nodes.label: Special Leave to Appeal (Article 136)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Under Article 136, the Supreme Court can grant special leave to appeal from any judgment or order passed by any court or tribunal in India (except military tribunals). This is a discretionary power and gives the SC wide appellate jurisdiction. Makes the SC the ultimate court of appeal in the country.

nodes.label: Judiciary-Parliament Conflict
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Recurrent conflict over scope of fundamental rights, Parliament amending power, right to property, and scope of judicial review. Intensified during 1967-1973. Key issues: Can Parliament abridge fundamental rights? Can amendments violate basic structure? Can judiciary intervene in legislative privileges? Resolved partially by Kesavananda ruling.

nodes.label: India as Union of States
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Article 1(1) declares India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States. The term Union implies that Indian federation is not the result of an agreement among states and no state has the right to secede. States and territories are specified in the First Schedule. India has single citizenship unlike some federations.

nodes.label: Federalism with Strong Central Government
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Indian Constitution creates a strong central government to stem disintegration and bring about social/political change. Centre controls economic and financial powers, can alter state boundaries, has emergency powers that centralize authority, controls all-India services (IAS, IPS), and has residuary powers. States have immense responsibilities but meagre revenue sources.

nodes.label: Emergency Provisions and Federalism
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Constitution has powerful emergency provisions that can turn the federal polity into a highly centralised system. During emergency, Parliament assumes power to make laws on State List subjects. Power becomes lawfully centralised. These provisions were designed to deal with extraordinary situations threatening national unity and integrity.

nodes.label: President's Rule (Article 356)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Provides for President rule when state government cannot function according to constitutional provisions. Results in takeover of state government by Union. Must be ratified by Parliament. Can be extended up to three years. Governor recommends dismissal. Sparingly used till 1967, frequently misused after. SC ruled its constitutional validity can be examined by judiciary (Bommai case).

nodes.label: Role of Governor in Centre-State Relations
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Governor is not elected but appointed by central government, making the office controversial. Can recommend dismissal of state government and dissolution of assembly. Can reserve state bills for President assent. Role becomes more controversial when different parties rule at centre and state. Sarkaria Commission recommended strictly non-partisan appointments.

nodes.label: Demands for State Autonomy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: States demand more powers and autonomy from the centre. Four dimensions: legislative (more powers from division of powers), financial (independent revenue sources), administrative (less central control over machinery), cultural/linguistic (opposition to Hindi domination, preservation of regional languages). Tamil Nadu, Punjab, West Bengal have been prominent in these demands.

nodes.label: Interstate Disputes
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Two major types: border disputes and river water disputes. Maharashtra-Karnataka dispute over Belgaum, Manipur-Nagaland border dispute, Punjab-Haryana over Chandigarh. River water disputes: Cauvery (Tamil Nadu-Karnataka), Narmada (Gujarat-MP-Maharashtra). Judiciary acts as arbitrator but these are fundamentally political disputes requiring negotiation.

nodes.label: River Water Disputes
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Disputes over sharing river waters between states are serious as they affect drinking water and agriculture. Cauvery dispute between Tamil Nadu and Karnataka is a major example. River water tribunals set up to settle such disputes under Article 262. Some disputes have reached the Supreme Court. Narmada dispute involves Gujarat, MP and Maharashtra.

nodes.label: Special Provisions for Certain States
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Constitution provides differential treatment to some states given their peculiar social and historical circumstances. Article 371 provides special provisions for NE states (Assam, Nagaland, Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram) due to distinct tribal populations. Also for Himachal Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Goa, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Sikkim. Reflects asymmetric federalism.

nodes.label: Article 370 -- Special Status of J&K
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Gave Jammu and Kashmir greater autonomy. Concurrence of state required for laws on Union and Concurrent lists. J&K had its own constitution and flag. No emergency for internal disturbances without state concurrence. Directive Principles did not apply. Amendments under Article 368 only with J&K government concurrence. In practice, autonomy was less than the language suggests due to presidential orders.

nodes.label: All-India Services
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Common services for the entire territory of India including IAS and IPS. Officers serve in state administration but are under control of central government. States cannot take disciplinary action or remove these officers. This is a centralising feature of Indian federalism. Ensures integrated administrative system across the country.

nodes.label: Financial Relations -- Centre and States
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Economic and financial powers are centralised in hands of central government. Revenue-generating items under Union control. States dependent on grants and financial assistance from centre. Planning led to considerable centralisation of economic decision-making. Union government uses discretion in giving grants and loans, leading to charges of discrimination against opposition-ruled states.

nodes.label: Article 257 -- Executive Power of Union over States
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Executive power of every state shall be so exercised as not to impede or prejudice the exercise of executive power of the Union. Executive power of Union extends to giving directions to a state as may appear necessary. Establishes supremacy of Union executive power over State executive power.

nodes.label: Parliament Power to Alter State Boundaries
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Parliament is empowered to form new states by separation of territory, unite two or more states, alter boundaries or even names of states. Only needs to secure views of concerned state legislature (not consent). This power shows that existence of states including territorial integrity is in hands of Parliament -- a major unitary feature.

nodes.label: Seventh Schedule
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Contains the three legislative lists -- Union List, State List, and Concurrent List -- that divide powers between Centre and States. The division of subjects forms the core of the federal scheme. Any dispute about which list a subject falls under is resolved by the judiciary based on constitutional provisions.

nodes.label: Asymmetric Federalism
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Unlike the constitutional symmetry of American federalism, Indian federalism is constitutionally asymmetric. Different states have different legal status and prerogatives. Special provisions exist for J&K (Art 370), NE states (Art 371), and other states. Reflects the diverse historical and social circumstances of different regions.

nodes.label: Local Government
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Government at village and district level closest to common people. Involves day-to-day life and problems of ordinary citizens. Based on the principle that local knowledge and local interest are essential for democratic decision making. Strengthens democratic processes by enabling participation and accountability at the grassroots level.

nodes.label: Panchayats in Directive Principles
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Before the 73rd Amendment, local government was mentioned in the Directive Principles of State Policy (Article 40) as a policy directive. Being a DPSP, this provision was non-justiciable and only advisory. Local government was a State subject. The 73rd and 74th amendments elevated local government from a mere directive to a constitutional mandate.

nodes.label: Ambedkar on Village Panchayats
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was not enthusiastic about village panchayats. He felt that the faction and caste-ridden nature of rural society would defeat the noble purpose of local government at the rural level. This contrasted with Gandhi view of village self-governance. This tension influenced the initially weak constitutional provisions for local government.

nodes.label: Constitution as a Living Document
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The Indian Constitution keeps responding to situations and circumstances arising from time to time. It is dynamic, open to interpretations, and able to respond to changing situations. It is not a frozen or static rulebook. Both political practice and judicial rulings have shown maturity and flexibility in implementing the Constitution.

nodes.label: Constitutional Amendment Procedure
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Article 368 provides for amendment of the Constitution. Three methods: (1) Simple majority of Parliament (like ordinary law) for some articles, (2) Special majority in both Houses separately for most amendments, (3) Special majority plus ratification by half of state legislatures for federal provisions. Only Parliament can initiate amendments. No joint session provision for amendment bills. President must give assent -- cannot send back for reconsideration.

nodes.label: Special Majority
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Required for constitutional amendments under Article 368. Two conditions must be met simultaneously: (1) majority of total membership of the House, and (2) two-thirds of members present and voting. In Lok Sabha with 545 members, minimum 273 must support. Both Houses must pass separately. Ensures broad consensus across political parties for any amendment.

nodes.label: Ratification by State Legislatures
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: For amendments affecting federal structure, distribution of powers, representation, or fundamental rights, special majority is not sufficient. Legislatures of at least half the states must also pass the amendment bill by simple majority. Protects federal structure by ensuring states participate in amending process. Only consent of half (not all) states is required.

nodes.label: Amendments by Simple Majority
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Many constitutional articles can be amended by a simple law of Parliament with no special procedure. Indicated by wording by law in articles. Examples: Article 2 (admission of new states), Article 3 (formation/alteration of states). These parts of the Constitution are very flexible. No difference between such amendment and ordinary law.

nodes.label: Balance between Rigidity and Flexibility
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Indian Constitution combines both rigid and flexible features. Flexible: some provisions amendable by simple majority, no referendum needed, no separate constitutional commission required. Rigid: special majority needed for most amendments, state ratification for federal provisions, basic structure cannot be amended. This balance ensures protection from unnecessary changes while allowing needed modifications.

nodes.label: Technical/Administrative Amendments
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: First group of amendments that are clarifications, explanations, and minor modifications making no substantial difference. Examples: increasing retirement age of HC judges from 60 to 62 (15th amendment), increasing judges salaries (55th amendment), periodic extension of SC/ST reservation in legislatures by 10 years. Amendments only in legal sense, not in substance.

nodes.label: Amendments from Differing Interpretations
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Second group of amendments arising when judiciary and government interpret Constitution differently. Parliament amends to establish one particular interpretation as authentic. Especially frequent during 1970-1975 when Parliament repeatedly amended to overcome adverse judicial interpretations on fundamental rights vs. directive principles, right to property, and amending power.

nodes.label: Amendments through Political Consensus
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Third group of amendments based on consensus among political parties reflecting evolving political philosophy. Post-1984 examples: anti-defection (52nd amendment), voting age reduction from 21 to 18 (61st amendment), 73rd and 74th amendments for local government, and reservation-related amendments (77th, 81st, 82nd). Shows Constitution evolving with societal consensus.

nodes.label: Basic Structure and Constitutional Evolution
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The basic structure doctrine has shaped constitutional evolution since 1973. Sets limits to Parliament amending power while allowing amendments to all other parts. Judiciary is final authority on what constitutes basic structure. The doctrine itself is an example of a living constitution -- no mention in text but emerged from judicial interpretation. Has been further elaborated in subsequent cases.

nodes.label: Constitutional Evolution through Judicial Interpretation
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Judiciary has contributed to informal amendments by interpreting provisions in new ways. Key examples: 50% ceiling on reservations, creamy layer concept for OBC reservations, expansion of right to education, right to life and liberty, minority educational institution rights. These rulings changed understanding of the Constitution without formal amendments.

nodes.label: Parliamentary Sovereignty vs. Constitutional Supremacy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Recurring tension in Indian constitutional development. Parliament claims supremacy as representative of the people. But the Constitution limits this through judicial review and basic structure doctrine. Sovereignty of elected representatives is the basis of amendment procedure, but judiciary ensures amendments do not violate basic structure. Balance maintained through mutual restraint.

nodes.label: Pattern of Constitutional Amendments
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Over 100 amendments in 75+ years. 1970-1990 saw the most amendments. Period 1974-1976 had 10 amendments in just 3 years (Congress dominance with 352 seats). Again 2001-2003 saw 10 amendments in 3 years (coalition era). Amendment frequency is not dependent on nature of majority alone -- reflects genuine constitutional needs across political configurations.

nodes.label: Philosophy of the Constitution
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The Constitution is based on a moral vision and political philosophy. It is liberal, democratic, egalitarian, secular, federal, open to community values, sensitive to needs of minorities and historically disadvantaged groups, and committed to building a common national identity. All underpinned by commitment to peaceful and democratic means of social transformation.

nodes.label: Individual Freedom
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Central commitment of the Constitution with roots going back to Rammohan Roy in early 19th century who protested against curtailment of press freedom. Freedom of expression, freedom from arbitrary arrest (opposing the Rowlatt Act), and freedom of conscience are integral parts. Every INC resolution from 1885 onwards mentioned individual rights as a non-negotiable value.

nodes.label: Social Justice
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Indian liberalism is linked to social justice, unlike classical western liberalism which privileges individual rights over social justice. Best exemplified by constitutional provisions for reservations for SC/ST. Constitution makers believed mere granting of right to equality was insufficient to overcome age-old injustices. India had affirmative action two decades before the US Civil Rights Movement (1964).

nodes.label: Respect for Diversity and Minority Rights
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Constitution encourages equal respect between communities. Recognises community-based rights unlike many western liberal constitutions. Right of religious communities to establish and run educational institutions receiving state aid. India is a land of multiple cultural communities, making it necessary to ensure no one community systematically dominates others.

nodes.label: Indian Secularism (Principled Distance)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Indian secularism differs from western mutual exclusion model. Two departures: (1) Recognises rights of religious communities, not just individuals -- freedom of religion for both individuals and communities, (2) State may intervene in religion to promote equality and social justice (e.g., abolition of untouchability). State maintains principled distance -- can help or hinder religious communities depending on which promotes liberty, equality, and justice.

nodes.label: Universal Adult Franchise
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A major achievement of the Indian Constitution. Adopted despite widespread traditional hierarchies believed impossible to eliminate. Indian nationalism always conceived of a political order based on will of every member. Constitution of India Bill (1895) already declared every citizen born in India had right to vote. Motilal Nehru Report (1928) reaffirmed universal franchise. Adopted at a time when even stable western democracies had only recently extended suffrage to women.

nodes.label: Asymmetric Federalism as Constitutional Philosophy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Unlike American constitutional symmetry, Indian Constitution has constitutionally embedded differences between legal status of different states. Articles 370 (J&K) and 371 (NE states) anticipate the concept of asymmetric federalism. Part of the original design to give certain regions special status based on their unique historical circumstances. India is now a multi-lingual federation treating all major linguistic groups as equals.

nodes.label: Common National Identity
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Constitution reinforces a common national identity compatible with distinct religious or linguistic identities. Balances various identities while preferring common identity under certain conditions. Rejected separate electorates based on religion not because they fostered difference but because they endangered healthy national life. Goal was to evolve true fraternity and one community (Sardar Patel).

nodes.label: Procedural Achievements of the Constitution
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Two key procedural achievements: (1) Faith in political deliberation -- Constituent Assembly debates show inclusive approach, willingness to modify preferences based on reasons rather than self-interest, recognition of creative value in disagreement. (2) Spirit of compromise and accommodation -- not all compromises are bad; trading off one value partially for another through free deliberation among equals is morally commendable.

nodes.label: Substantive Achievements of the Constitution
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Five core substantive achievements: (1) Reinforcing liberal individualism in a community-oriented society, (2) Upholding social justice without compromising individual liberties, (3) Commitment to group rights and multiculturalism, (4) Universal adult franchise despite hierarchies, (5) Asymmetric federalism to address regional diversity. These features together form the political philosophy of the Constitution.

nodes.label: Constitution as Means of Democratic Transformation
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Constitutions exist not only to limit power but to empower the traditionally deprived. Nehru saw the Constituent Assembly as a nation on the move, throwing away the shell of its past social structure. Constitution designed to break shackles of traditional social hierarchies and usher in a new era of freedom, equality, and justice. Provides peaceful democratic means for social change.

nodes.label: Criticisms of the Indian Constitution
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Three major criticisms: (1) Unwieldy -- too large a document (addressed: many details included that other countries handle separately), (2) Unrepresentative -- Constituent Assembly chosen by restricted franchise, not universal suffrage (addressed: wide range of opinions were represented, Dalits identify with it), (3) Alien/borrowed -- based on western constitutions (addressed: it was innovative borrowing, not blind borrowing; selective adaptation creating alternative modernity).

nodes.label: Limitations of the Constitution
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Three notable limitations: (1) Centralised idea of national unity, (2) Has glossed over some important issues of gender justice, particularly within the family, (3) Unclear why basic socio-economic rights were relegated to Directive Principles rather than made fundamental rights. These limitations are not serious enough to jeopardise the overall philosophy.

nodes.label: Selective Adaptation (Not Blind Borrowing)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Indian Constitution is modern and partly western but represents innovative borrowing, not blind copying. When western modernity interacted with Indian cultural systems, a hybrid alternative modernity emerged. Dalits effectively adopted modern legal systems as early as 1841 to address questions of dignity. Constitution amalgamates western and traditional Indian values through selective adaptation.

nodes.label: Affirmative Action (Reservations)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Constitutional commitment to caste-based affirmative action to overcome age-old injustices. Includes reservation of seats in legislatures and reservation in public sector jobs for SC/ST. India was ahead of other nations -- affirmative action in US began only after 1964 Civil Rights Movement, almost two decades after being constitutionally entrenched in India.

nodes.label: Multiculturalism in the Constitution
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Constitution upholds commitment to group rights -- the right to expression of cultural particularity. Against background of inter-communal strife, framers were willing to face challenges of what later came to be known as multiculturalism. Recognises community values, linguistic and religious diversity, and provides institutional mechanisms for their protection.

nodes.label: Western vs. Indian Conception of Secularism
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Western secularism: mutual exclusion of state and religion; state neither helps nor hinders religions. Indian secularism: principled distance -- state can intervene in religion to abolish practices like untouchability; can also assist religious educational institutions. Reason: religiously sanctioned customs were so deeply rooted that without active state intervention, there was no hope of dissolution.

nodes.label: Constituent Assembly Debates
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Indian Constitution must be read in conjunction with Constituent Assembly Debates to understand justification of values embedded in it. Debates show vast range of issues and opinions were represented. Important for understanding the original intent and philosophy behind constitutional provisions. History of Constitution is still very much a history of the present -- values and ideals have not fundamentally changed.

nodes.label: Liberal Individualism in Indian Context
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Constitution reinforces and reinvents forms of liberal individualism in a society where community values are often hostile to individual autonomy. Two streams of Indian liberalism: first stream started by Rammohan Roy (individual rights, women rights); second stream (K.C. Sen, Justice Ranade, Swami Vivekananda) introduced social justice within orthodox Hinduism. Both streams inform the Constitution.

nodes.label: Sovereignty
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Supreme authority of the state over its territory, free from external control. Internal sovereignty means authority over citizens; external sovereignty means independence from other states. Central to statehood.

nodes.label: Negative Liberty
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Freedom from interference or external constraints. Absence of obstacles, barriers, or coercion by others. Associated with Isaiah Berlin. The state should not interfere in individual choices. Classical liberal position.

nodes.label: Positive Liberty
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Freedom to achieve one's potential, self-mastery, and self-realization. Requires enabling conditions like education, healthcare, minimum standard of living. The state must create conditions for individuals to be truly free.

nodes.label: Civil Liberties
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Freedoms that protect individuals from government overreach. Include freedom of speech, assembly, religion, movement. Constitutionally guaranteed in India under Part III. Different from political rights like right to vote.

nodes.label: Social Equality
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Absence of discrimination based on caste, religion, race, gender, or birth. Requires elimination of social hierarchies and untouchability. Indian Constitution addresses through Articles 15, 17, and anti-discrimination provisions.

nodes.label: Equality of Opportunity
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: All persons should have equal chance to develop their talents and compete on merit. Requires removing barriers of birth, caste, and wealth. May require affirmative action to level the playing field. Article 16 guarantees this in public employment.

nodes.label: Liberal View of Equality
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Liberals emphasize equality of opportunity and equal rights under law. Rawls' 'justice as fairness' permits inequalities only if they benefit the least advantaged. Balances freedom with equality through procedural fairness.

nodes.label: Veil of Ignorance
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Rawls' thought experiment: if people did not know their position in society (class, gender, abilities), what principles of justice would they choose? They would choose equality because anyone could end up disadvantaged. Foundational concept in political theory.

nodes.label: Difference Principle
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Rawls' principle that social and economic inequalities are justified only if they benefit the least advantaged members of society. Not absolute equality but structured inequality that helps the worst off.

nodes.label: Distributive Justice
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Fair allocation of resources, benefits, and burdens in society. Key question: what is a just distribution? Different theories offer different answers: utilitarian (maximize total welfare), libertarian (protect property rights), egalitarian (reduce inequality).

nodes.label: Rawls' Theory of Justice
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Justice as fairness. Two principles: (1) each person has equal right to most extensive basic liberties compatible with similar liberty for others, (2) inequalities permitted only if they benefit the least advantaged. Foundational modern theory of justice.

nodes.label: Utilitarian Justice
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Greatest good for the greatest number. Associated with Bentham and Mill. Criticized for potentially justifying sacrifice of minority rights if it maximizes overall welfare. Does not adequately protect individual rights.

nodes.label: Libertarian Justice
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Justice requires protecting individual rights, especially property rights. Robert Nozick's 'entitlement theory': distribution is just if it results from voluntary exchanges. Minimal state intervention. Opposes redistribution through taxation.

nodes.label: Ambedkar on Social Justice
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Ambedkar championed social justice for oppressed castes. Argued political democracy without social democracy is meaningless. Designed constitutional provisions for reservation, abolition of untouchability. Social justice as constitutional mandate, not charity.

nodes.label: Global Justice
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Extending justice beyond national boundaries. Includes fair international trade, addressing global poverty, climate justice, rights of migrants. NCERT discusses how globalization raises questions about justice across borders.

nodes.label: Open Society
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Society where individuals are free to question, criticize, and reform social institutions. Karl Popper's concept. Contrasted with closed societies based on rigid hierarchies and absolute authority. Democratic societies aspire to be open.

nodes.label: Special Treatment for Disadvantaged
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Differential treatment of historically disadvantaged groups to achieve substantive equality. Includes reservations, scholarships, land reforms. Justified as corrective justice for past wrongs and structural inequality. Not reverse discrimination but compensatory justice.

nodes.label: Legal Rights
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Rights created and enforced by law of the state. Can be changed by legislation. Different from fundamental rights which require constitutional amendment. Right to property is now a legal right (not fundamental) in India after 44th Amendment.

nodes.label: Moral Rights
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Rights based on moral or ethical principles rather than law. May not be legally enforceable but carry moral weight. Example: right to be treated with dignity. Can evolve into legal rights over time through social movements.

nodes.label: Human Rights
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Universal rights belonging to all humans regardless of nationality, ethnicity, or other status. Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) lists right to education, equal access to public service, right to food. UPSC 2011 tested UDHR rights.

nodes.label: Citizenship by Birth
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Jus soli principle: acquiring citizenship by being born in the territory. India grants citizenship by birth to those born in India (with conditions tightened over time through amendments). Not the only route to citizenship.

nodes.label: Citizen vs Non-Citizen
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Citizens have full political rights (vote, hold office). Non-citizens have some fundamental rights (Art 14, 21) but not all (Art 15, 16, 19 are for citizens only). Right to property (Art 300A) available to any person, not just citizens.

nodes.label: Global Citizenship
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Idea that people have responsibilities beyond national borders. Environmental issues, human rights, poverty are global concerns. Challenges traditional state-based citizenship. Does not replace national citizenship but supplements it.

nodes.label: Statelessness
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Condition of not being considered a citizen by any state. Rohingya crisis is a prominent example. Stateless persons lack legal protection, cannot vote, face difficulty accessing services. UN Convention on Statelessness (1961) addresses this.

nodes.label: Refugees and Citizenship
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Refugees flee persecution but are not citizens of host country. Tension between state sovereignty and humanitarian obligations. India is not a signatory to 1951 Refugee Convention but has hosted refugees from Tibet, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka.

nodes.label: Citizenship Amendment Issues
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Citizenship Act 1955 has been amended multiple times, tightening conditions for citizenship by birth. Debates over who qualifies as citizen reflect tension between inclusive and exclusive conceptions of national identity.

nodes.label: Dual Citizenship Debate
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Some countries allow citizens to hold citizenship of two nations. India does not allow dual citizenship but has OCI (Overseas Citizen of India) card as a compromise. OCI is not actual citizenship; holders cannot vote or hold constitutional posts.

nodes.label: Nation
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A large group of people sharing common culture, history, language, or ethnicity and identifying as a political community. Different from state (political-legal entity) and nation-state (when nation and state boundaries coincide). Imagined community (Benedict Anderson).

nodes.label: Nation-State
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Political unit where the boundaries of the nation and state coincide. Most modern states claim to be nation-states but are actually multi-national (India has many nations/communities within one state). Ideal type rarely achieved in practice.

nodes.label: Civic Nationalism
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: National identity based on shared political values, citizenship, and common institutions rather than ethnicity. French model: anyone who accepts republican values is French. More inclusive. India's constitutional nationalism is largely civic.

nodes.label: Ethnic Nationalism
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: National identity based on shared ethnicity, language, religion, or culture. German Romantic model: blood and soil. More exclusive. Can lead to xenophobia and ethnic cleansing when taken to extremes. NCERT warns about its dangers.

nodes.label: Indian Nationalism
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Unity in diversity: Indian nationalism accommodates linguistic, religious, and cultural diversity within one nation. Constitutional patriotism rather than ethnic nationalism. Challenged by communalism, regionalism, and secessionism.

nodes.label: Regionalism
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Strong identification with a particular region over national identity. Can be positive (preserving regional culture) or negative (secessionism). Indian federalism accommodates legitimate regional aspirations within national framework.

nodes.label: Dangers of Nationalism
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Extreme nationalism can lead to militarism, xenophobia, ethnic cleansing, and war. Nazi Germany and fascist movements used hyper-nationalism. NCERT warns that nationalism must be tempered by democratic values and respect for human rights.

nodes.label: Cultural Diversity and Nationalism
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Multi-cultural nations like India face the challenge of building national identity while respecting diversity. Assimilationist model (suppress differences) vs pluralist model (accommodate differences). India follows the pluralist model through constitutional protections.

nodes.label: Tagore's Critique of Nationalism
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Rabindranath Tagore criticized aggressive nationalism as a form of organized selfishness. Advocated universal humanism over narrow nationalism. Believed that India's contribution should be spiritual and cultural, transcending national boundaries.

nodes.label: Gandhi's Vision of Nationalism
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Gandhi's nationalism was inclusive, non-violent, and rooted in swaraj (self-rule). Combined national freedom with social reform. Rejected narrowly defined nationalism; envisioned India welcoming all cultures. Non-violence as method and goal.

nodes.label: Secularism
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Principle of separation between religion and state. State does not promote any religion and treats all religions equally. Two models: Western (strict wall of separation) and Indian (principled distance). Part of basic structure of Constitution.

nodes.label: Western Secularism
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Strict separation of church and state (American model). State has nothing to do with religion; religion is entirely private matter. No state funding of religious institutions. Based on Enlightenment rationalism. Critiqued for ignoring religious minorities' needs.

nodes.label: Indian Secularism
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Principled distance: state is not strictly separated but maintains equal respect for all religions. State can intervene in religious practices to ensure reform (abolish untouchability, sati). State can fund religious institutions equally. More substantive than Western model.

nodes.label: Principled Distance
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Indian state's approach: neither complete separation nor identification with any religion. State may engage with religion when necessary (social reform, protecting minorities) but maintains distance from religious domination. Coined by political theorist Rajeev Bhargava.

nodes.label: Religious Freedom
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Freedom to practice, profess, and propagate religion (Articles 25-28). Subject to public order, morality, health. State can regulate economic/political activities associated with religious practice. Includes freedom to not follow any religion.

nodes.label: Inter-Religious Domination
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Domination of one religious community over another. Secularism opposes this: majority should not impose its religion on minorities. Indian secularism protects minorities from majoritarian religious domination. Constitutional safeguards in Articles 25-30.

nodes.label: Intra-Religious Domination
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Oppression within a religion: caste hierarchy in Hinduism, patriarchy in all religions, orthodox vs reformist factions. Indian secularism allows state to intervene within religions to protect individual rights and promote social reform.

nodes.label: Secular State
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: State with no official religion, treats all religions equally, does not discriminate on basis of religion. Added to Preamble by 42nd Amendment (1976). Originally implicit in Constitution; the word 'secular' made it explicit.

nodes.label: Communalism as Threat to Secularism
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Communalism treats religious identity as primary political identity, directly opposing secularism. Communal riots, hate speech, and religious polarization undermine secular fabric. Constitution provides safeguards but secularism requires active civic commitment.

nodes.label: Personal Laws
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Laws governing marriage, divorce, inheritance, adoption based on religion. Hindu, Muslim, Christian, Parsi personal laws exist in India. Seen by some as protecting religious identity, by others as violating equality and women's rights.

nodes.label: State and Religious Reform
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Indian state has intervened in religious practices: abolishing untouchability, sati, child marriage. Hindu Code Bills reformed Hindu personal law. This distinguishes Indian secularism from Western: state actively reforms unjust religious practices rather than just staying out.

nodes.label: Toleration
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Willingness to accept beliefs or practices different from one's own. Weaker than equal respect: toleration merely allows others to exist. Indian secularism aspires beyond toleration to equal respect and principled distance.

nodes.label: Critiques of Secularism
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Critiques include: (1) anti-religious bias (secularism seen as hostility to religion), (2) Western import (not suited to Indian context), (3) vote-bank politics (selective appeasement of minorities), (4) interventionist (state interference in religious matters). NCERT addresses these systematically.

nodes.label: Nehru's Vision of Secularism
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Nehru saw secularism as essential for democratic India. Opposed communal politics. Envisioned India where religion is personal and state is neutral. His secularism was closer to Western model of separation but adapted to Indian plurality.

nodes.label: Gandhi's Religious Pluralism
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Gandhi was deeply religious but believed all religions lead to truth. Sarva Dharma Sambhava: equal respect for all religions. Different from Nehru's secular approach; Gandhi integrated religious values into politics while opposing religious exclusivism.

nodes.label: Articles 25-28 (Religious Freedom)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Art 25: freedom of conscience, profess/practice/propagate. Art 26: manage religious affairs. Art 27: no tax for religious promotion. Art 28: no religious instruction in state-funded institutions. Together these establish India's secular framework.

nodes.label: Structural Violence
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Violence built into social structures: poverty, caste discrimination, gender inequality, lack of access to healthcare/education. No visible perpetrator but systematic harm. Concept by Johan Galtung. Addressing this is key to positive peace.

nodes.label: Non-Violence (Ahimsa)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Principle of not causing harm through physical force. Gandhi's central philosophy: non-violence as both strategy and moral principle. Satyagraha as non-violent resistance. Not passive submission but active resistance without violence.

nodes.label: Gandhi's Philosophy of Peace
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Peace through non-violence and truth (satyagraha). Means are as important as ends: violent means cannot achieve peaceful ends. Peace is not just absence of conflict but presence of justice. Influenced global peace movements including Martin Luther King Jr.

nodes.label: Pacifism
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Complete opposition to war and violence. No war is justified regardless of cause. Gandhi's ahimsa is a form of principled pacifism. Criticized for being impractical when facing extreme aggression like fascism.

nodes.label: Terrorism
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Use of violence against civilians for political purposes. NCERT discusses how terrorism threatens peace and security. State response must balance security with protecting civil liberties. No universally agreed definition exists.

nodes.label: Right to Development
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: UN Declaration on Right to Development (1986): development is a human right. Every person and all peoples are entitled to participate in and benefit from development. States have duty to create conditions for development. Third generation right.

nodes.label: Logic of Deterrence
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Both superpowers possessed nuclear weapons capable of inflicting unacceptable destruction on each other, making full-scale war unlikely. Neither side could afford to initiate war since the other retained enough weapons to retaliate devastatingly.

nodes.label: New International Economic Order (NIEO)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Proposed reform of global trading system to benefit LDCs. Originated from UNCTAD report of 1972. Demanded LDC control over natural resources, access to Western markets, reduced technology costs. Faded by late 1980s due to opposition from developed countries.

nodes.label: Constraints on US Power
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Three constraints: institutional architecture (separation of powers limits executive military action), open society (domestic public scepticism), and NATO (alliance of democracies that can moderate US behaviour). No single power can militarily balance the US.

nodes.label: European Integration Timeline
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: 1951: ECSC by six states. 1957: EEC and Euratom (Treaties of Rome). 1973: UK, Denmark, Ireland join. 1979: First European Parliament elections. 1985: Schengen Agreement. 1992: Maastricht Treaty establishes EU. 2002: Euro introduced. 2004: Ten new members including former Warsaw Pact states.

nodes.label: ASEAN Way
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Form of interaction among ASEAN members that is informal, non-confrontationist, and cooperative. Respect for national sovereignty is critical. Distinguishes ASEAN from supranational organisations like the EU.

nodes.label: Rise of China
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: China has been the fastest growing economy since reforms began in 1978. Projected to overtake US as world's largest economy by 2040. Accession to WTO in 2001. Largest destination for FDI. However, faces unemployment, environmental degradation, and inequality.

nodes.label: South Asia as a Region
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Includes Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka. Bounded by Himalayas in north, Indian Ocean in south. Diversity in political systems but widespread aspiration for democracy. India is centrally located and borders all others.

nodes.label: Democracy in Bangladesh
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Part of Pakistan until 1971. Sheikh Mujib-ur Rahman led the independence movement through Awami League. Gained independence after 1971 India-Pakistan war. Constitutional democracy based on secularism, democracy, socialism. Military rule under Ziaur Rahman and Ershad. Multiparty democracy since 1991.

nodes.label: Sri Lanka Ethnic Conflict
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Conflict between majority Sinhala and Tamil minority. LTTE fought armed struggle from 1983 demanding Tamil Eelam. India signed accord in 1987 and sent IPKF (1987-90) which failed. Despite civil war, Sri Lanka maintained democracy, high GDP, and human development indicators.

nodes.label: UN Peacekeeping Operations
nodes.subject: polity
