nodes.detail: UN deploys peacekeeping forces in conflict zones worldwide. India has been a major contributor to peacekeeping missions. Operations run by Department of Peacekeeping Operations. Active in Congo, Cyprus, Lebanon, Sudan, Kosovo, and many others.

nodes.label: UN in a Unipolar World
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: UN cannot easily check US power as the sole superpower with veto. US is the largest financial contributor and the UN is located on US territory. However, UN provides space for dialogue and can moderate US attitudes and policies through discussion and compromise.

nodes.label: Traditional Security (External)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Greatest danger from military threats by another country endangering sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity. Government has three choices: surrender, deterrence, or defence. Force is both the principal threat and principal means of achieving security.

nodes.label: Traditional Security (Internal)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Newly independent countries faced threats from separatist movements and neighbour-instigated conflicts. Internal wars now make up over 95% of armed conflicts worldwide. Between 1946-1991, twelve-fold rise in civil wars. Cold War was responsible for about one-third of post-WWII wars.

nodes.label: Balance of Power
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: States are sensitive to power distribution and work to maintain favourable balance through military buildup, economic power, and technology. Countries assess potential threats based on neighbours' capabilities even without obvious aggression intentions.

nodes.label: Alliance Building
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Coalition of states coordinating actions to deter or defend against military attack. Most alliances formalised in treaties. Based on national interests and can change. Example: US backed Afghan militants against USSR in 1980s but attacked them after 9/11.

nodes.label: Disarmament
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Requires all states to give up certain weapons. The 1972 Biological Weapons Convention (BWC) and 1992 Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC) banned production and possession. Over 155 states acceded to BWC and 181 to CWC, including all great powers.

nodes.label: Confidence Building Measures (CBMs)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Process where countries share information on defence matters with rivals to prevent war through misunderstanding. Includes sharing military intentions, plans, force composition, and deployment. Designed to ensure rivals do not go to war by mistake.

nodes.label: Global Security
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Emerged in 1990s in response to global threats like warming, terrorism, and epidemics. No country can resolve these alone. Requires international cooperation. Sea level rise threatens Maldives, Bangladesh, Thailand.

nodes.label: Human Rights as Security Issue
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Three types: political rights (speech, assembly), economic and social rights, rights of colonised/indigenous minorities. Debate on whether UN should intervene in violations. Iraq's invasion of Kuwait, Rwanda genocide, and East Timor killings prompted intervention debates.

nodes.label: Environment in Global Politics
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Environmental issues became political from the 1960s. Club of Rome published Limits to Growth in 1972. UNEP began promoting coordinated responses. Key questions: who causes degradation, who pays the price, who takes corrective action. Deeply political questions about power distribution.

nodes.label: Global Commons
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Areas outside sovereign jurisdiction requiring common governance: Earth's atmosphere, Antarctica, ocean floor, and outer space. Management influenced by North-South inequalities. Key issue is technology and industrial development determining who benefits.

nodes.label: Antarctica
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: 14 million sq km continent with 90% of terrestrial ice and 70% of planetary freshwater. Some countries claim sovereign rights (UK, Argentina, Chile) while most consider it global commons. 1959 Antarctic Treaty limits activities to research, fishing, tourism. 1991 Environmental Protocol provides protection.

nodes.label: Water Conflicts
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Freshwater scarcity points to water disputes as leading source of 21st century conflicts. Disagreements over shared rivers (irrigation, dams, pollution). Examples: Israel-Syria-Jordan over Jordan River, Turkey-Syria-Iraq over Euphrates. Countries sharing rivers often involved in military conflicts.

nodes.label: Indigenous Peoples and Rights
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Approximately 30 crore indigenous peoples worldwide. In India, Scheduled Tribes (8% of population). Loss of land is the most obvious threat to survival. World Council of Indigenous Peoples formed in 1975. First of 11 indigenous NGOs with UN consultative status.

nodes.label: Environmental Movements
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Among most vibrant social movements globally. Include forest movements (South), anti-mining campaigns (Philippines vs WMC), anti-dam movements (Narmada Bachao Andolan in India, Franklin River in Australia). Non-violence is a shared idea in Indian environmental movements.

nodes.label: Brundtland Report (Our Common Future)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: 1987 report that warned traditional patterns of economic growth were not sustainable long-term. Coined the widely used concept of sustainable development. Set the stage for the 1992 Earth Summit.

nodes.label: Sacred Groves in India
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Parcels of uncut forest vegetation in the name of deities or spirits. Model of community-based resource management. Preserve biodiversity and cultural diversity. Characteristics of common property resource systems. Threatened by expansion and new forest policies.

nodes.label: Congress Dominance (1952-1967)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: INC won 364 of 489 Lok Sabha seats in 1952, and maintained three-fourths of seats in 1957 and 1962 elections. It dominated both centre and states. This dominance was due to freedom struggle legacy, organisational spread, charismatic leadership, and the first-past-the-post system that magnified vote share into seat share.

nodes.label: Congress as Social and Ideological Coalition
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Congress functioned as a platform accommodating diverse groups -- peasants and industrialists, all castes and classes, multiple religions and languages. It was also an ideological coalition containing conservative, radical, right, left and centre factions. This internal pluralism was the key to its dominance.

nodes.label: First-Past-The-Post System
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: India's electoral system where the candidate with most votes wins. In 1952, Congress got 45% votes but 74% seats. The non-Congress votes were divided among many parties, artificially boosting Congress seat count. This explains the gap between vote share and seat share.

nodes.label: Mixed Economy Model
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: India chose neither pure capitalism nor pure socialism. Agriculture, trade and industry remained partly in private hands while the state controlled heavy industries, provided infrastructure, regulated trade and intervened in agriculture. Criticised from both left and right.

nodes.label: Agriculture vs Industry Debate
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Fundamental debate in Indian planning. Gandhians like J.C. Kumarappa and leaders like Chaudhary Charan Singh wanted agriculture at the centre. Nehru-Mahalanobis school favoured heavy industries. Second Plan industrial emphasis was criticised for urban bias.

nodes.label: Kerala Model of Development
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Alternative decentralised planning model focused on education, health, land reform, food distribution and poverty alleviation. Despite low per capita income, Kerala achieved near-total literacy, high life expectancy, low infant mortality and high healthcare access.

nodes.label: Article 51 - International Peace
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Directive Principle of State Policy on Promotion of international peace and security. Directs the state to promote peace, maintain just relations between nations, foster respect for international law, and encourage settlement of disputes by arbitration. Constitutional basis for India's foreign policy.

nodes.label: Non-Congressism
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Strategy given by socialist leader Ram Manohar Lohia where ideologically different opposition parties would unite against Congress. Led to formation of anti-Congress fronts and Samyukt Vidhayak Dal (SVD) governments in states. Based on the argument that Congress rule was undemocratic and anti-poor.
nodes.chapter_title: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System

nodes.label: Congress Syndicate
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Informal group of powerful Congress organisational leaders who controlled the party. Led by K. Kamraj, included S.K. Patil, S. Nijalingappa, N. Sanjeeva Reddy, Atulya Ghosh. Backed both Shastri and Indira Gandhi for PM but expected them to follow their advice. Indira gradually sidelined them.
nodes.chapter_title: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System

nodes.label: Garibi Hatao (Remove Poverty)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Indira Gandhi's famous election slogan for the 1971 elections. Focused on public sector growth, land ceilings, urban property ceilings, and abolition of princely privileges. Built a new support base among the disadvantaged -- landless labourers, Dalits, Adivasis, minorities, women and unemployed youth.
nodes.chapter_title: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System

nodes.label: Defection Politics (Aya Ram Gaya Ram)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: After the 1967 elections, defections by legislators played a major role in making and unmaking governments. The expression 'Aya Ram Gaya Ram' originated from Gaya Lal, a Haryana MLA who changed party thrice in a fortnight in 1967. This eventually led to the anti-defection law (52nd Amendment, 1985).
nodes.chapter_title: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System

nodes.label: SVD (Samyukt Vidhayak Dal) Governments
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Coalition governments formed by non-Congress parties after the 1967 elections. Ideologically incongruent coalitions -- e.g., Bihar SVD included socialists (SSP, PSP), CPI on the left and Jana Sangh on the right. Most did not survive long due to internal contradictions.
nodes.chapter_title: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System

nodes.label: Non-Party Political Formations
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: In the 1970s-80s, many politically active groups lost faith in electoral politics and chose to step outside party politics. Formed voluntary organisations working with rural poor, Dalits and Adivasis. Did not contest elections but participated in politics through direct action and mass mobilisation.

nodes.label: Green Revolution and its Discontents
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Farmers of Punjab, Haryana and western UP benefited from Green Revolution policies of the late 1960s. Sugar and wheat became main cash crops. But in the mid-1980s, crisis hit due to liberalisation. This generated the farmers movements led by BKU and other organisations.

nodes.label: Northeast Movements
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The isolated and underdeveloped Northeast region presented challenges of national integration. Nagaland granted statehood after China war. Manipur and Tripura got legislative assemblies. Mizoram saw insurgency in 1966 (Mizo National Front) but achieved peace through the Mizo Accord of 1986 and statehood in 1987.

nodes.label: Era of Coalition Politics
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Since 1989, no single party has won a clear Lok Sabha majority. Every government has been either a coalition or a minority government with outside support. Regional parties became crucial kingmakers. NDA (BJP-led) and UPA (Congress-led) emerged as the two main coalition frameworks.

nodes.label: Rise of BJP
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: After Jana Sangh merged into Janata Party (1977) and then re-emerged as BJP (1980), it initially adopted Gandhian Socialism. After poor results in 1984, shifted to Hindutva ideology. Used the Ayodhya issue and Ram Janmabhoomi movement for mobilisation. Emerged as largest party by 1996 and led NDA governments from 1998.

nodes.label: Political Rise of OBCs
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Long-term development of OBC communities as a political force. Support for Congress among backward castes declined, creating space for parties like Janata Dal, Samajwadi Party, RJD. Mandal Commission implementation made OBC identity politically salient. All major parties now accept OBC reservations.

nodes.label: Historical Factors of Diversity
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Diversity developed through centuries of migration, trade, and conquest. People travelled for new lands, trade, or to escape famine and war. As they settled, their languages, food, music, and religions became a mix of old and new, creating unique regional cultures.

nodes.label: Geographical Factors of Diversity
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: People adapt their lives to their geographical area -- coastal living differs from mountainous or desert regions. Geography determines food, clothing, occupation, and culture. Kerala (coastal, spice-rich) and Ladakh (mountainous desert) illustrate this.

nodes.label: Caste-based Discrimination
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: In the caste system, communities were placed in a hierarchy. Upper castes saw themselves as superior. Untouchables were forced into specific occupations, denied entry to temples, wells, and schools. The practice denied dignity, respect, and equal rights to lower castes.

nodes.label: Untouchability
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The practice of treating certain caste groups as impure or unworthy. Untouchables were not allowed to enter upper-caste homes, temples, or draw water from village wells. Their children were segregated in schools. Now legally abolished and considered a crime.

nodes.label: Dalit
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A term meaning broken, used by people of so-called lower castes to address themselves, preferred over untouchable. It reflects how social prejudices and discrimination have broken them. The government refers to this group as Scheduled Castes (SC).

nodes.label: Constitutional Equality
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The Constitution of India establishes that all people are equal. Untouchability is legally abolished as a crime. People are free to choose their work. Government jobs are open to all. The government must take specific steps to realise equality for poor and marginal communities.

nodes.label: India as a Secular Country
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: India became a secular country where people of different religions and faiths have freedom to practise and follow their religion without fear of discrimination. No single language, religion, or festival is compulsory. The government must treat all religions equally.

nodes.label: Striving for Equality
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The freedom struggle included struggles by Dalits, women, tribals, and peasants against inequalities. Dalits fought for temple entry, women demanded education rights, peasants and tribals fought moneylenders. Equality requires continuous effort and positive government action.

nodes.label: Scheduled Castes (SC)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The official government designation for communities historically subjected to untouchability. The Constitution provides special provisions for their upliftment, including reservation in government jobs and educational institutions.

nodes.label: Poverty and Discrimination
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Poor people lack resources for basic needs and face discrimination in offices, hospitals, and schools. Some experience double discrimination -- being poor and belonging to groups whose culture is not valued. Poverty, not religion, is often the cause of educational exclusion.

nodes.label: Laws and Government
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The government makes laws that everyone must follow. It has the power to enforce decisions. Without laws, the government decision-making power would be ineffective. Citizens can approach courts if they believe a law is not being followed.

nodes.label: Representative Democracy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Modern democracies where people do not participate directly but choose representatives through elections. These representatives meet and make decisions for the entire population. India follows this model of democratic governance.

nodes.label: Participation in Democracy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A key element of democracy where people elect leaders through voting, and also participate through rallies, dharnas, strikes, signature campaigns, and social movements. Regular elections (every five years in India) limit government power and ensure accountability.
nodes.chapter_title: Key Elements of a Democratic Government

nodes.label: Regular Elections
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: In India, governments are elected for fixed five-year periods. They must be re-elected to continue in power. This is the moment when people sense their power in a democracy. Regular elections limit government power and ensure accountability.
nodes.chapter_title: Key Elements of a Democratic Government

nodes.label: Social Movements
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Organised efforts by people to challenge the government and its functioning. Members of minority communities, Dalits, Adivasis, women, and others participate through social movements when they cannot participate through conventional means.
nodes.chapter_title: Key Elements of a Democratic Government

nodes.label: Forms of People Participation
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Beyond voting, people participate in democracy through dharnas, rallies, strikes, signature campaigns, letters to newspapers, and criticising government policies. Newspapers, magazines, and TV also play a role in discussing government issues and responsibilities.
nodes.chapter_title: Key Elements of a Democratic Government

nodes.label: Government Accountability
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: In a democracy, the government is responsible to the people and must explain its actions. If people express disapproval (e.g., against electricity price hikes through rallies and campaigns), the government may be forced to withdraw its decisions.
nodes.chapter_title: Key Elements of a Democratic Government

nodes.label: Urban Livelihoods
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: People in cities earn their living through diverse activities: street vending, market shops, factory work, office employment, and daily wage labour. Employment can be self-employed, casual, or permanent and regular. India has over 5000 towns and 27 big cities.

nodes.label: Street Vendors
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Nearly one crore street vendors work in urban India. They sell goods or provide services (repair, cobbling, barbering) on streets. They are self-employed, organise their own work, use temporary structures, have no security, and can be evicted by police. Hawking zones have been suggested to protect them.

nodes.label: Market Businesspersons
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Owners of permanent shops in city markets, licensed by the Municipal Corporation. They are self-employed but employ supervisors and helpers. They source goods from various cities and use advertising. The Municipal Corporation decides weekly closing days for markets.

nodes.label: Permanent and Regular Workers
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Workers with regular salaries in offices, factories, or government departments. They get benefits including provident fund savings for old age, holidays (Sundays, national holidays, annual leave), and medical facilities for family. They cannot be easily dismissed.

nodes.label: Self-Employment
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: People who work on their own without being employed by anyone. Includes street vendors, cycle-rickshaw pullers, and market shopkeepers. They organise their own work, decide purchases, and manage their businesses independently.

nodes.label: Call Centres
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A new form of urban employment in big cities. Centralised offices dealing with consumer problems regarding goods and services like banking and ticket booking. India has become a major centre for both Indian and foreign companies due to English-speaking workforce available at lower wages.

nodes.label: Rural to Urban Migration
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: People migrate from villages to cities in search of work and better income. Cycle-rickshaw pullers, construction workers, and factory workers often come from rural areas where they could not find regular employment. They send money back to their families in villages.

nodes.label: Equality in Democracy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Equality is a key feature of democracy influencing all aspects of its functioning. The Indian Constitution recognises every person as equal irrespective of caste, religion, tribe, educational and economic background. Equality encompasses political, social, and economic dimensions.

nodes.label: Article 15 - Prohibition of Discrimination
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Article 15 prohibits discrimination by the State on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth. It also ensures equal access to shops, public restaurants, hotels, places of entertainment, wells, tanks, bathing ghats, and roads maintained by the State.

nodes.label: Equality Before Law
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Every person from the President to an ordinary citizen must obey the same laws. This principle, enshrined in Article 14 of the Indian Constitution, ensures that no one is above the law and forms the foundation of the rule of law in India.

nodes.label: Abolition of Untouchability
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Article 17 of the Indian Constitution abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form. The enforcement of any disability arising from untouchability is an offence punishable by law. This was a landmark constitutional measure to address caste-based discrimination.

nodes.label: Dignity and Self-Respect
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Dignity refers to thinking of oneself and others as worthy of respect. When persons are treated unequally based on caste, religion, sex, or economic status, their dignity is violated. The Constitution aims to ensure that every citizen can live with dignity.

nodes.label: Religious Discrimination
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Despite constitutional protections, religious minorities face discrimination in housing, employment, and social life. The Ansari case illustrates how Muslims can be denied housing based on religion even when they have financial means to pay.

nodes.label: Right to Access Public Places
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Every person has access to all public places including playgrounds, hotels, shops, markets, wells, roads, and bathing ghats. This right under Article 15(2) prevents social exclusion and ensures public spaces are available to all irrespective of caste or religion.

nodes.label: Communicable Diseases and Public Health
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Diseases spread through water, food, and air such as TB, malaria, jaundice, cholera, diarrhoea. 21 percent of communicable diseases in India are water-borne. Government must organise prevention campaigns with public participation, as individual action is insufficient.
nodes.chapter_title: Role of the Government in Health

nodes.label: Gender Gap in Literacy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: In the 1961 census, 40 percent of males but only 15 percent of females were literate. By 2011, figures grew to 82 percent for males and 65 percent for females. The gap has narrowed but persists. SC, ST, and Muslim girls have even higher dropout rates.

nodes.label: SC/ST Girls School Dropout
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Girls from Dalit (SC) and Adivasi (ST) backgrounds leave school at rates higher than the category of all girls. Muslim girls are even less likely to complete primary school, staying only about three years compared to four for others. Poverty, distance, and discrimination are key factors.

nodes.label: Media and Democracy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: In a democracy, media plays a vital role in providing news and discussing events, enabling citizens to learn how government works and take informed action. Citizens can write to ministers, organise protests, or start campaigns based on media information. Balanced, independent media is essential.

nodes.label: Balanced Reporting
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A balanced report discusses all points of view of a story and leaves readers to make up their minds. Most media fails to provide balanced stories due to business interests, desire to make stories interesting, or wanting to build support for particular positions.

nodes.label: Independent Media
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: No one should control or influence medias coverage of news. Independent media is important in a democracy because citizens take action based on the information media provides. However, media is far from independent due to government control and business influence.

nodes.label: Censorship
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: When the government prevents news items, movie scenes, or song lyrics from being shared with the public. The worst period of censorship in India was during the Emergency between 1975-1977. While government no longer censors news coverage, it still censors films.

nodes.label: Media Setting the Agenda
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Media decides what stories to focus on and what is newsworthy, thereby influencing public thoughts, feelings, and actions. Fashion Week made front pages while slum demolitions in Mumbai went unnoticed. Media positively highlighted pesticides in cola drinks, forcing accountability.

nodes.label: Media and Big Business
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Big business houses own radio, TV, and newspapers. They advertise products through media, which promotes these products to readers and viewers. People buy products, sending money back to big business. This cycle means media reporting against advertisers becomes difficult.

nodes.label: Local and Community Media
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Local groups have started their own media recognising mainstream media ignores small issues of ordinary people. Community radio informs farmers about crop prices. Khabar Lahriya, a fortnightly run by eight Dalit women in Chitrakoot, UP, reports on Dalit issues and violence against women in Bundeli language.

nodes.label: Public Protest
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: When a large number of people come together and openly state their opposition to some issue. Methods include organising rallies, starting signature campaigns, and blocking roads. Public protests are an important way citizens hold the government accountable in a democracy.

nodes.label: Neighbourhood Shops
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Permanent shops near homes available on any day of the week. Buyer and seller typically know each other. These shops provide goods on credit, allowing payment later. Include dairies, departmental stores, stationery shops, medical stores, and roadside hawkers.

nodes.label: Chain of Markets
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A series of markets connected like links in a chain through which products pass from producer to final consumer. Goods are produced in factories, farms, and homes but reach consumers through multiple traders. This chain links faraway places and enables distribution.

nodes.label: Wholesale Trader
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Traders who buy goods in large quantities (25 to 100 kilos) and sell to other traders. Every city has wholesale market areas where goods first reach before being supplied to retailers. They participate in auctions and store goods in godowns.

nodes.label: Retailer
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The trader who finally sells goods to the consumer. Could be a trader in a weekly market, a hawker in the neighbourhood, or a shop in a shopping complex. The last link in the chain of markets connecting producer to consumer.

nodes.label: Hawker
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Roadside sellers who do not have permanent shops. They sell vegetables, fruits, plastic items, and other goods at lower prices than permanent shops. They purchase from wholesale traders and sell directly to consumers, forming an important part of the market chain.

nodes.label: Credit System in Markets
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Neighbourhood shops allow buyers to purchase goods and pay later, typically at the start of the next month. Both buyer and seller maintain notebooks recording amounts owed. This system relies on trust between known parties and is not available in malls or weekly markets.

nodes.label: Markets Beyond Physical Spaces
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Buying and selling takes place beyond traditional marketplaces. Orders can be placed by phone or Internet with home delivery. Sales representatives visit doctors to sell medicines. Factories buy components from other factories. Much commerce happens invisibly behind final products.

nodes.label: Producer-Consumer Gap
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Producers on farms and in factories do not sell directly to consumers. Multiple intermediaries -- wholesale traders, distributors, retailers -- connect producers to consumers. Each link adds cost. This gap means consumers may not know where goods originate or how they are produced.

nodes.label: Parliamentary Form of Government
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: India adopted a parliamentary system where elected representatives form the government. Based on universal adult suffrage. The executive is accountable to the legislature. The Constituent Assembly believed this would break caste, class, and gender hierarchies.

nodes.label: Right to Freedom of Religion
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Every person has the right to practise, profess, and propagate the religion of their choice. Integral to India's secular character and protects religious minorities.

nodes.label: Universal Adult Suffrage
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The Constitution guarantees the right to vote to all adult citizens regardless of social background. Every citizen can also contest elections. Meant to break traditional caste, class, and gender hierarchies.

nodes.label: Tyranny of the Majority
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Where the majority continuously enforces decisions that exclude minorities. The Constitution prevents this through protective rules. Applies to both inter-community and intra-community domination.

nodes.label: State vs Government Distinction
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: 'State' represents a sovereign people occupying a definite territory. 'Government' administers laws and changes with elections. Government is one part of the State. The two cannot be used interchangeably.

nodes.label: Strategy of Distancing
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: First way Indian secularism works: the State distances itself from religion. India is not ruled by a religious group, does not support any one religion. Government spaces like courts, police stations, schools cannot display or promote any one religion.

nodes.label: Strategy of Non-Interference
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Second way Indian secularism works: the State respects religious sentiments by making exceptions for particular communities. Example: Sikhs wearing turbans exempt from helmet laws. This respects religious practices while maintaining secular principles.

nodes.label: Strategy of Intervention
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Third way Indian secularism works: the State intervenes in religious affairs to end discriminatory practices. The Constitution bans untouchability. State may intervene in personal laws for equal inheritance rights. Also supports religious communities through financial aid for schools.

nodes.label: Religious Domination
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Discrimination, coercion, or persecution of religious minorities by a majority with access to State power. Secularism aims to prevent this. Historical examples include persecution of Jews in Hitler's Germany and treatment of minorities in theocratic states.

nodes.label: American Secularism
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The First Amendment of the US Constitution prohibits the legislature from making laws respecting establishment of religion or prohibiting free exercise. Strict separation - neither State nor religion can interfere in affairs of the other. Differs from India's principled distance model.

nodes.label: Freedom to Interpret Religion
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Protecting individuals' freedom to exit their religion, embrace another, or interpret religious teachings differently. Separation of State and religion is needed so dominant factions cannot impose a single interpretation using State power.

nodes.label: Coercion by State
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The use of force by a legal authority like the State. If a majority religious group gains State power, it could use coercion to discriminate against minorities, prevent their religious practice, or commit violence.

nodes.label: Government Schools and Religion
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Government schools cannot promote any one religion in morning prayers or celebrations. This policy of equal treatment applies to government but not private schools. Religious holidays allow home celebration rather than institutional promotion.

nodes.label: Abolition of Untouchability
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The Indian Constitution bans untouchability as State intervention in religious affairs to end intra-community domination. Upper-caste domination of lower castes through untouchability violates Fundamental Rights. Example of State intervening in religion for equality.

nodes.label: People's Participation in Democracy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Citizens' role extends beyond voting. Through newspapers, media, local meetings, and protests, citizens participate in governance. People's involvement helps Parliament perform its representative functions. Citizens can criticise and hold MPs accountable.
nodes.chapter_title: Why Do We Need a Parliament

nodes.label: Independence of Judiciary
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Key Constitutional feature ensuring legislature and executive cannot interfere in judicial work. Judges appointed with minimal interference. Very difficult to remove once appointed. Allows courts to protect Fundamental Rights and check misuse of power.

nodes.label: Dispute Resolution
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Judiciary resolves disputes between citizens, between citizens and government, between two state governments, and between centre and states. Essential for maintaining rule of law and federal balance.

nodes.label: Appellate System
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: India has an integrated judicial system where higher court decisions bind lower courts. A person can appeal to a higher court if they believe a lower court judgment is unjust. Cases can move from Trial Court to High Court to Supreme Court.

nodes.label: Right to Life (Article 21) - Expanded Interpretation
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Article 21 expanded through court interpretations to include Right to Health (Hakim Sheikh case), Right to Food (PUCL case, mid-day meals), Right to Livelihood (Olga Tellis case), Right to Water, Right to Education, Right to Shelter. Demonstrates Constitution as living document.

nodes.label: Access to Justice
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Courts available to all in principle but access difficult for the poor due to costs, paperwork, and time. 'Justice delayed is justice denied.' PIL was introduced to address this gap. Shortage of judges contributes to delays.

nodes.label: Role of Police in Investigation
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Police investigate complaints by recording witness statements and collecting evidence. They form an opinion and file a chargesheet if evidence points to guilt. Police are NOT judges - they cannot decide guilt or innocence. Investigation must follow law and respect human rights. Police cannot torture, beat, or shoot during investigation.

nodes.label: Fair Trial
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Essential elements: accused gets copy of chargesheet; charged with offence defined in law; trial in open court; trial in presence of accused; defended by lawyer; opportunity to cross-examine prosecution witnesses; presumption of innocence; prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt; judge decides on evidence alone.

nodes.label: Article 22 - Rights of Arrested Persons
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Fundamental Rights of arrested persons: right to be informed of offence at arrest; right to be presented before magistrate within 24 hours; right not to be ill-treated or tortured; confessions in police custody cannot be evidence; boys under 15 and women cannot be called to police station only for questioning.

nodes.label: D.K. Basu Guidelines
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Supreme Court guidelines for arrest, detention, and interrogation. Requirements include: police must wear visible ID and name tags; arrest memo with time and date attested by witness; arrested person's right to inform relative or friend; notification to family within 8-12 hours if they live outside district.

nodes.label: Presumption of Innocence
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A fundamental principle of criminal law. The judge assumes the accused is innocent until prosecution proves guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The burden of proof lies with the prosecution, not the accused. This protects individuals from wrongful conviction.

nodes.label: Article 21 and Fair Procedure
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Article 21 guaranteeing Right to Life states that a person's life or liberty can be taken away only by following a reasonable and just legal procedure. A fair trial ensures Article 21 is upheld. Without fair trial, the right to life would be meaningless.

nodes.label: Bail
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A court order allowing an arrested person's temporary release pending trial, usually requiring a surety (guarantee). If the accused cannot arrange surety, they may remain in jail despite the bail order. Bail protects the liberty of an accused who has not yet been proven guilty.

nodes.label: Marginalisation
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Being forced to the fringes of society due to language, customs, religion, poverty, or social status. Economic, social, cultural, and political factors work together. Marginalised groups lack access to resources and opportunities and cannot assert their rights. Leads to disadvantage and powerlessness.

nodes.label: Constitutional Safeguards for Minorities
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The Constitution provides safeguards to religious and linguistic minorities as Fundamental Rights. These protect minority cultures from being dominated by the majority. Size can be a disadvantage leading to marginalisation. Safeguards protect against discrimination, disadvantage, and cultural domination.

nodes.label: Invoking Fundamental Rights
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Marginalised groups draw on Fundamental Rights in two ways: first, insisting on rights to force government to recognise injustice; second, insisting government enforce laws. Their struggles have influenced government to frame new laws in keeping with the spirit of Fundamental Rights.

nodes.label: Article 17 - Abolition of Untouchability
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: States that untouchability has been abolished. No one can prevent Dalits from educating themselves, entering temples, or using public facilities. Practising untouchability is a punishable crime. A crucial provision for Dalit dignity and equality.

nodes.label: Law and Social Justice
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Government makes laws to protect workers, consumers, and producers from unfair market practices. Through making, enforcing, and upholding laws, the government controls activities of private companies to ensure social justice. Many laws have basis in Fundamental Rights.

nodes.label: Workers' Rights
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Include right to work, right to fair wage, decent work conditions, and right to form unions. The Right against Exploitation prohibits forced labour and bondage. Constitution also prohibits child labour under 14 in factories, mines, and hazardous employment. Workers' unions bargain collectively for better conditions.

nodes.label: Enforcement of Safety Laws
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Government is supposed to ensure safety laws are implemented and Right to Life under Article 21 is not violated. In Bhopal, safety laws were lax and even weak laws were not enforced. Government officials approved unsafe procedures and allowed the plant in a populated area despite safety violations.

nodes.label: Consumer Protection Laws
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Laws requiring goods to meet prescribed quality and safety standards to protect consumers from harm (electrical appliances, food, medicines). Laws keeping essential goods affordable (sugar, kerosene, foodgrains) to protect the poor. Market regulation prevents exploitation of consumers.

nodes.label: Constitution as Living Document
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The Right to Life (Article 21) has been continuously expanded through citizen efforts and court interpretations to include rights to health, food, livelihood, water, education, shelter, and clean environment. This intrinsic flexibility allows new interpretations, making the Constitution a living document that evolves with democratic ideals.

nodes.label: Democracy (Basic Definition)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A form of government that allows people to choose their rulers. Leaders elected by people rule the country, and people have freedom to express views, organise, and protest. Most prevalent form of government in the contemporary world.

nodes.label: Military Coup
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Overthrow of a democratically elected government by the armed forces. The Chile coup of 1973 against Allende by Pinochet is a classic example. Military coups are a recurring threat to democracy worldwide.

nodes.label: Referendum
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A direct vote by the people on a specific political question. In Chile, Pinochet's 1988 referendum backfired when people voted no. Can be used by both democratic and authoritarian regimes.

nodes.label: International Organisations and Democracy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Bodies like UN, IMF, World Bank exercise global influence but are not fully democratic. UN Security Council veto power and IMF weighted voting raise questions about democracy at the global level.

nodes.label: Martial Law
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Imposition of military control over civilian government. In Poland, General Jaruzelski imposed martial law in December 1981, imprisoning thousands of Solidarity members and suppressing freedoms.

nodes.label: Features of Non-Democratic Government
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: People cannot choose or change rulers; no freedom to express opinions, form political associations, or organise protests; power not based on popular mandate. Includes military dictatorships, one-party states, absolute monarchies.

nodes.label: Constitution
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Supreme law of the country that determines rights of citizens, powers of government, and how government should function. Set of written rules accepted by all people, laying down limits on government power and expressing aspirations of the people.

nodes.label: Preamble to Indian Constitution
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Opening statement declaring India as a Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic. Promises justice (social, economic, political), liberty (of thought, expression, belief, faith, worship), equality (of status and opportunity), and fraternity (assuring dignity of individual and unity of nation).

nodes.label: Socialist (in Preamble)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Wealth is generated socially and shared equally by society. Government shall regulate ownership of land and industry to reduce socio-economic inequalities. Added by 42nd Amendment (1976).

nodes.label: Democratic Republic
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Head of state (President) is elected, not hereditary. Government derives authority from the people through elections. Both representative democracy at centre/state and direct democracy at local level through panchayats.

nodes.label: Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Four pillars of Indian democracy from the Preamble. Justice: social, economic, political. Liberty: of thought, expression, belief, faith, worship. Equality: of status and opportunity. Fraternity: dignity of individual and unity of nation.

nodes.label: Sources of Indian Constitution
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Indian Constitution drew from multiple sources: British parliamentary system, US Bill of Rights, Irish Directive Principles, French ideals of liberty and republic, Canadian federation model, Australian concurrent list concept. Synthesis of global constitutional wisdom.

nodes.label: Constitutional Amendment
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Process to change the Constitution. Indian Constitution provides for amendments under Article 368. Some require simple majority, others two-thirds majority plus ratification by half the states. Over 100 amendments made since 1950, showing it is a living document.

nodes.label: Election Campaign
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Period of 2 weeks between announcement and voting when candidates contact voters. Model Code of Conduct applies: no bribing, no government resources for campaign, no appeals to caste/religion, campaign stops 48 hours before voting.

nodes.label: Political Competition
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Competition among parties and candidates for electoral victory. Creates incentives for parties to serve people's needs. Despite creating factionalism, competition ensures accountability - like market forces ensuring good service.

nodes.label: Independent Candidate
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A candidate who contests elections without being nominated by any political party. Can contest from any constituency. In India, independent candidates rarely win Lok Sabha elections but are more common at local levels.

nodes.label: Political Institutions
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Arrangements in democracy for governing. Include legislature, executive, and judiciary. Constitution lays down powers and functions of each. Working with institutions involves rules, regulations, meetings, and committees that ensure democratic governance.

nodes.label: Coalition Government
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Government formed by alliance of multiple parties when no single party wins majority. Common in India's multi-party system. PM must manage coalition partners, making governance more complex but also more representative.

nodes.label: Abolition of Untouchability
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Article 17 abolishes untouchability in all forms and makes its practice punishable. Untouchability includes any belief or practice that discriminates against people based on caste. Despite constitutional prohibition, social practice continues in some areas.

nodes.label: What are Rights
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Claims of a person over fellow beings, society, and government. Must be reasonable, available equally to others, recognised by society, and sanctioned by law. Rights come with obligations to respect others' rights. Natural/moral rights become legal rights when written into law.

nodes.label: Expanding Scope of Rights
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Rights expand over time through legislation, judicial interpretation, and constitutional amendments. Examples: Right to Education, Right to Information, environmental rights. Courts have expanded Right to Life (Article 21) to include right to livelihood, clean environment, and privacy.

nodes.label: Fundamental Rights
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Inspired by US Bill of Rights and Irish Constitution. Six categories: Right to Equality, Right to Freedom, Right against Exploitation, Right to Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, Right to Constitutional Remedies. Abolition of untouchability (Article 17) a landmark provision.

nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Non-justiciable guidelines from Irish Constitution. Include promoting welfare, minimising inequalities, providing adequate livelihood, equal pay, protecting environment. Debated whether these were merely 'pious wishes' or moral obligations. Ambedkar defended them as novel and necessary.

nodes.detail: Every adult citizen over 21 (now 18) given right to vote regardless of property, education, gender or caste. Radical step for a largely illiterate, poor society. Some members doubted capacity of masses. Ambedkar called political democracy meaningless without social and economic democracy.

nodes.detail: Constitution established a Union of States (not a federation). Three lists: Union, State and Concurrent. Residuary powers with Centre. Strong central government with emergency provisions. Debate between supporters of strong centre (for national unity) and those wanting state autonomy.

nodes.label: Secularism in Constitution

nodes.detail: Constitution guarantees freedom of religion (Articles 25-28) while allowing state to regulate religious practices for social reform. No state religion. State treats all religions equally. 'Secular' explicitly added to Preamble by 42nd Amendment (1976). Different from Western secularism.

nodes.label: Reservation Policy

nodes.detail: Constitutional provisions for reservation of seats in legislatures and posts in government services for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. Initially for 10 years, extended periodically. Debated intensely: supporters argued it addressed historical injustice, critics feared it would entrench caste.

nodes.label: Three Lists of the Constitution
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Constitution balanced Centre-State relations through Union List (taxes, defence, foreign affairs), State List (education, health) and Concurrent List (forests, agriculture) with joint Centre-State responsibility.

nodes.label: Belgium's Power Sharing Model
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Belgium (population ~1 crore) has Dutch (59%), French (40%), German (1%) speakers. Constitutional amendments (1970-1993) created: equal Dutch-French ministers in central government, state governments with constitutional powers, Brussels with equal community representation, and community governments for cultural matters.

nodes.label: Sri Lanka's Majoritarianism
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Sinhala majority (74%) imposed dominance: Sinhala Only Act (1956), preferential university/job policies for Sinhalas, constitutional protection of Buddhism. Alienated Tamil minority (18%), leading to civil war. Example of what happens when power is not shared.

nodes.label: Community Government (Belgium)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Unique Belgian innovation: elected by people of one language community (Dutch, French, German) regardless of where they live. Has power over cultural, educational, and language-related matters. Ensures linguistic minorities have a voice in governance.

nodes.label: Equal Wages Act
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Law providing that equal wages should be paid for equal work regardless of gender. However, in practice women are paid less than men in almost all areas. Shows the gap between legal provision and social reality.

nodes.label: Isaiah Berlin
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Political philosopher who distinguished between negative liberty (freedom from interference) and positive liberty (freedom to achieve potential) in his essay 'Two Concepts of Liberty' (1958). Warned that positive liberty could be misused to justify authoritarian control.

nodes.label: John Rawls
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: American philosopher (1921-2002). 'A Theory of Justice' (1971). Veil of ignorance thought experiment. Two principles: equal basic liberties for all, and inequalities only if they benefit the least advantaged (difference principle).

nodes.label: Robert Nozick
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: American philosopher (1938-2002). 'Anarchy, State, and Utopia' (1974). Entitlement theory of justice: holdings are just if legitimately acquired. Argues against redistributive taxation as forced labor. Key counterpoint to Rawls.

nodes.label: Benedict Anderson
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Political scientist who conceptualized nations as 'imagined communities' in his 1983 book. Argues nations are socially constructed through shared media, print capitalism, and common narratives. Not imaginary but imagined in the sense that members will never know most fellow members.

nodes.label: Ernest Renan
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: French philosopher who defined nation as a 'daily plebiscite': continuous affirmation of desire to live together. Nation is not just shared past but shared future aspirations. Rejected purely racial or linguistic definitions of nation.

nodes.label: Rajeev Bhargava
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Indian political theorist who articulated the concept of 'principled distance' as the distinctive feature of Indian secularism. Argues Indian secularism addresses both inter-religious and intra-religious domination, unlike Western secularism.

nodes.label: Mahbub ul Haq
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Pakistani economist who created the Human Development Index (HDI) for UNDP. Argued that people are the real wealth of nations, not GDP. Partnered with Amartya Sen to develop the human development paradigm.

nodes.label: India's Security Strategy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Four components: military capability (wars with Pakistan and China, nuclear tests 1974 and 1998); strengthening international norms (NAM, NIEO, Kyoto Protocol, UN peacekeeping); internal security (democracy to address separatism in Nagaland, Punjab, Kashmir); economic development to reduce poverty.

nodes.label: India's Opposition to NPT
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: India consistently opposed the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (1968) as discriminatory because it legitimised the monopoly of five nuclear weapons powers. India refused to sign NPT and later CTBT. India's nuclear doctrine professes no-first-use and credible minimum deterrence.

nodes.label: Ladakh - Cultural Diversity
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A mountainous desert in eastern Jammu and Kashmir. Known for pashmina wool from special goats. Buddhism reached Tibet via Ladakh (called Little Tibet). Islam was introduced over 400 years ago. A trade route with passes for caravans carrying textiles, spices, silk, and carpets.

nodes.label: Constitution of India
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The document that laid out the rules by which the nation would function. Writers were aware of historical discrimination and how people had struggled against it. It sets out a vision and goals to ensure all people of India are considered equal.

nodes.label: Indian Constitution - Basic Rules
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The Indian Constitution lays down the basic rules or laws that have to be followed by everyone, including the government and the people. Conflicts and differences have to be resolved according to these laws.
nodes.chapter_title: Key Elements of a Democratic Government

nodes.label: Hector Pieterson - Soweto Uprising
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A schoolboy from South Western Township (Soweto) who was shot by police on 16 June 1976 during protests against forced learning of Afrikaans language. Students wanted to learn their own language, Zulu. His death became a symbol of the anti-apartheid struggle.
nodes.chapter_title: Key Elements of a Democratic Government

nodes.label: Indian Constitution
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The foundational legal document that lays down basic rules and regulations for people and the government. It recognises equality of all persons, prohibits discrimination, abolishes untouchability, and ensures access to public places for all citizens.

nodes.label: Primary Health Centre (PHC)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Government health centre covering many villages in rural areas. Supervised by doctors who oversee village health workers and nurses. Forms part of the three-tier public health system along with village health centres and district hospitals.
nodes.chapter_title: Role of the Government in Health

nodes.label: Minimum Wages Act
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Law specifying that wages should not be below a minimum level. Protects workers, particularly farm labourers, construction workers, factory workers, and domestic workers. Minimum wages are revised upwards every few years. Without this law, employers would exploit workers' vulnerability due to high unemployment.

nodes.label: Mexico's PRI Dominance
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Mexico's PRI (Institutional Revolutionary Party) won every election from 1930 to 2000 using dirty tricks: forcing government employees to attend meetings, media bias, shifting polling booths, massive campaign spending. Not truly democratic despite holding elections.

nodes.label: Article 21 Evolution (A.K. Gopalan → Maneka)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: 'No person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.' A.K. Gopalan (1950) — narrow reading, no due process. Maneka Gandhi (1978) — 'procedure' must be fair/just/reasonable = substantive due process. Post-Maneka: right to livelihood, privacy, education, clean environment — expansive interpretation.

nodes.label: Article 14 — Equality Before Law
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Combines British 'equality before law' (Dicey, formal) and American 'equal protection of laws' (substantive). Permits reasonable classification (not class legislation). Basic structure element (Indra Sawhney 1992, Puttaswamy 2017). Gateway for non-arbitrariness review.

nodes.label: Article 32 — Heart and Soul of Constitution
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Ambedkar's 'without which this Constitution would be a nullity'. Writs — Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto. Only Article 32 itself a Fundamental Right. Cannot be suspended except during Emergency. Available only for enforcement of FRs.

nodes.label: Original Eight Schedules (1950)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Constitution originally had 8 schedules. 9th (1951, land reforms), 10th (1985, anti-defection), 11th (1992, panchayats), 12th (1992, municipalities) added later. Now 12 schedules total.
